newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Little sign of early end to Brazzaville conflict.
newsitem.headline: Little sign of early end to Brazzaville conflict.

text.p: Brazzaville's second war, as the bloody showdown between President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor has become known, entered its fifth week on Thursday with little sign of an end in sight.
The first "war" in the Congo Republic capital, ethnic and political clashes that followed a disputed 1993 parliamentary election, ran into 1994 and killed at least 2,000 people.
This time, a bloody remix of political and ethnic clashes with indiscriminate shelling, has killed hundreds more.

"In the short term, I just don't see talks taking place," says Richard Banegas, a researcher at CERI, a unit of the Paris Sciences Politiques institute. "The protagonists have got themselves into a cycle of violence."
Political analysts say Lissouba and ex-military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso seem to have little interest in negotiating.

Each leader, they add, sees this as his last chance for a stab at another term in office -- Sassou because he won't have the money to finance another campaign, Lissouba because he will be in his seventies if he misses out this time.
An announcement on Wednesday by Brazzaville mayor and national mediator Bernard Kolelas that hoped-for talks between the two factions would not go ahead, came as no surprise.
Brazzaville, shaken by mortar fire on Wednesday night, was quiet again on Thursday -- a now familiar pattern.
The showdown began on June 5 when the army surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militia.
As in 1993, the trigger for unrest was an election -- a now derailed July 27 presidential election.
This time, with Lissouba's mandate running out at the end of August, any solution must inevitably include another election.
A dispute over who should govern has complicated things. Lissouba says the constitution grants him a 90-day extension to allow elections. Sassou wants a transitional authority.
Another major problem is weapons. Both Sassou and Lissouba, security experts say, had stockpiles when the conflict began. Both have added to their stockpiles since it started.
Economic pressure offers little scope for leverage.
"We saw them send away a World Bank committee not so long ago," said CERI's Banegas.

The Congo Republic has a foreign debt of more than $5 billion, the highest per capita in Africa, but it is poised to get more revenue from the offshore oil fields of N'Kossa and Kitina after renegotiation of production sharing agreements.
This, economists say, will cut its dependence on foreign aid, currently about 20 percent of the state's financing needs.
What could sway the balance in the conflict is Kolelas, whose Ninja militia fought in 1993 but have stayed on the sidelines this time.
"The way the conflict develops in the future will depend on the attitude of Kolelas and his militia," said one pundit.

Kolelas, head of the Congolese Party for Democracy and Integral Development (MCDDI) and runner-up to Lissouba in the 1992 presidential election, has links with both sides. He also planned to stand again on July 27.
Politically, as mayor, he has cohabited with Lissouba. His cousin Philippe Bikinkita is interior and security minister.
His grass-root supporters have more affinities with Sassou.
"His militia were trained and financed by Sassou's people -- Kolelas owes his position as a warlord to Sassou," says CERI's Banegas. "In the long term his position will become untenable."

Kolelas has ignored shells that have landed in his Bacongo and Makelekele strongholds. "The only thing that will inspire him to take up arms is if Lissouba launches a fully fledged attack on Bacongo and Makelekele," said one diplomat.
"Why would anyone want to provoke someone who is preaching peace?" Kolelas himself asked in a French radio interview.
Some political analysts say he lacks the money to join the conflict. His main source of income, despite repeated denials, is unofficial ports he controls on the Congo river, they add.
Gabon's veteran president, Omar Bongo, has launched an international mediation bid. He is an old friend of Lissouba and ethnically close to him but his wife is Sassou's daughter Edith.
"In fact he's proving incapable of choosing between Lissouba, whom he prefers, and Sassou," said one diplomat.
Some pundits speculate that Laurent Kabila's Congo, just across the river, could get involved. "The only chance for a military solution is if Kabila steps in," said one diplomat.
Kabila's government has warned of retaliation if more shells hit Kinshasa but Kolelas plays down earlier "hits" as mistakes.
U.N. and Organisation of African Unity special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who is trying to pull together an African peacekeeping force, returned to Brazzaville on Thursday to seek a solution.
He is not alone. Kolelas says he too will pursue his mediation. "I think that both sides are sensitive to the suffering of our people and will do what is necessary to reach a consensus," he adds.
